references.text: The priest who performs the ritual with the red heifer must also wash his clothes and bathe in water, and remain unclean until evening—the same cleansing procedure as the one who burns the heifer.
The one who gathers the ashes of the heifer must also wash his clothes and remain unclean until evening, as part of the same cleansing ritual.
The same principle of washing clothes and remaining unclean until evening applies to the one who carries dead animals.
Washing clothes and bathing in water as a cleansing ritual, with uncleanness lasting until evening, is a recurring pattern in the law of purity.
The one who releases the goat to Azazel must also wash his clothes and bathe, and then return to the camp—parallel to the cleansing after burning the heifer.
The one who burns the sin offering and the burnt offering outside the camp on the Day of Atonement must wash his clothes and bathe—a direct parallel to the burning of the red heifer.
The Epistle to the Hebrews refers to the ashes of the heifer as cleansing for the purity of the flesh, and points to how Christ's blood provides a deeper cleansing.
